# APA redline — Buyer's draft (Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC) for Brightline Cabinetry LLC

Seller-side markup of §§2.4, 3.3, 4.12, 7.4(a)–(c), 8.2, 9.3. Verdict per section: **keep** or **change**, with proposed replacement language and reason. Only authorities in `library/INDEX.md` are cited; anything else is labeled unverified.

Deal math used throughout (assumption, see QUESTIONS.md): escrow of $310,000 = "10%" (APA §9.3) implies **Purchase Price ≈ $3,100,000** (310,000 / 0.10). The general cap (§7.4(b), 10%) is therefore ≈ $310,000, and the §4.12/fundamental cap (full price) is ≈ $3,100,000.

---

## §2.4 Earn-Out — **CHANGE**

**Buyer's draft (problem core):** "EBITDA ... as determined by Buyer in good faith in accordance with Buyer's accounting policies, consistently applied"; 40% of EBITDA over $700,000, max $400,000.

**Replacement language (proposed):**

> 2.4 Earn-Out. In addition to the Closing Payment, Buyer shall pay Seller an amount equal to 40% of the amount by which Adjusted EBITDA of the Business for the twelve months following Closing exceeds $700,000, up to a maximum of $400,000. "Adjusted EBITDA" means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of the Business, determined in accordance with GAAP consistently applied and consistent with the historical accounting practices used in the preparation of Seller's 2025 financial statements, and shall (i) exclude all allocations of Buyer's or its Affiliates' overhead, management fees, corporate charges, transaction costs, integration and restructuring costs, synergies, and any depreciation, amortization or other expense arising from purchase accounting or the transaction; (ii) include all costs of the spray-booth permit transition. Buyer shall (a) operate the Business (and each Business segment) in the ordinary course consistent with past practice and shall not take any action the primary purpose of which is to reduce or avoid the Earn-Out payment; (b) provide Seller monthly and annual financial statements for the Business and reasonable access to records and personnel to verify them; and (c) upon any sale or change of control of the Business or its assets during the Earn-Out period, pay Seller the maximum Earn-Out amount then unpaid. Any dispute over Adjusted EBITDA shall be submitted, within 30 days after receipt of the Earn-Out statement, to an independent nationally recognized accounting firm reasonably acceptable to both parties, whose determination is final and binding, with costs borne by the non-prevailing party.

**Why:** An earn-out measured by "EBITDA as determined by Buyer under Buyer's policies" lets the buyer allocate overhead, management fees, integration costs and purchase-accounting adjustments against the target and zero the earn-out; the protections above (defined accounting principles, exclusions, ordinary-course and no-purpose covenants, information/audit rights, neutral accountant, acceleration on resale) are the standard seller protections. *Lazard Technology Partners v. Qinetiq*, 114 A.3d 193 (Del. 2015); earnout_definitions.md.

**Economic note for Ray (show the arithmetic):** maximum payout requires EBITDA of $700,000 + $400,000 ÷ 0.40 = **$1,700,000** — more than double the $740,000 seller-prepared 2025 EBITDA. At exactly $740,000 the payout is 0.40 × ($740,000 − $700,000) = **$16,000**. Strip the add-backs (owner salary $180k, "one-time" legal $42k) and 2025 EBITDA is $740,000 − $180,000 − $42,000 = **$518,000**, i.e., $182,000 *below* the hurdle. The clause as drafted is close to worthless; do not give real consideration for it — trade it for a lower hurdle or more cash at closing.

---

## §3.3 Required Consents — **CHANGE (and populate Schedule 3.3)**

**Buyer's draft:** "Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the consents listed on Schedule 3.3 prior to Closing. (Schedule 3.3: 'None.')"

**Replacement language (proposed):**

> 3.3 Required Consents. (a) Schedule 3.3 lists each consent, approval or notice required under the Assigned Contracts and the shop lease in connection with the transactions contemplated hereby. Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain each consent listed on Schedule 3.3 prior to Closing. (b) It is a condition to each party's obligation to close that: (i) Hensley Homes has consented in writing to the assignment of the Master Supply Agreement; (ii) the landlord has consented in writing to assignment of the lease for 7700 Burleson Rd; and (iii) the City of Austin spray-booth permit application for Buyer has been accepted for processing.
>
> **Schedule 3.3 (proposed):** (1) Hensley Homes — MSA §18 consent, sole discretion (data room §1.1). (2) Landlord, 7700 Burleson Rd — lease §22 consent, not to be unreasonably withheld (data room §3.1). (3) Cascade Builders — assignment permitted to a successor to substantially all assets **upon notice**; written notice required, no consent (data room §1.2). (4) The 22 residential contracts are silent on assignment; no consent required as to rights (Restatement (Second) of Contracts §317), subject to confirmation that no engagement is personal-services dependent (Restatement §322; see QUESTIONS.md). (5) Governmental: City of Austin spray-booth permit — non-transferable; Buyer must reapply (30–60 days) (data room §4.1).

**Why:** "None" is false, and an efforts covenant pointing at an empty schedule allocates no risk while hiding a real closing failure. The Hensley clause bars assignment "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise," consent may be withheld in sole discretion, and a purported assignment is **void**; a clause of that kind is enforced according to its terms, so closing without consent is a breach and the 38%-of-revenue contract does not pass. *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§317, 322; anti_assignment_change_of_control.md. "Sole discretion" means expect a renegotiation ask from Hensley; decide now whether Ray will pay a concession (price/term) to keep the deal on schedule.

---

## §4.12 Employees and Contractors — **CHANGE**

**Buyer's draft:** flat rep that all individuals are properly classified and all taxes withheld/paid.

**Replacement language (proposed):**

> 4.12 Employees and Contractors. Except as set forth on Schedule 4.12, all individuals providing services to the Business have been properly classified as employees or independent contractors under applicable law, and Seller has withheld and paid all required taxes with respect to such individuals. Schedule 4.12 shall disclose: nine installers paid on Form 1099 in 2025 (aggregate $612,000) who use Brightline trucks and tools, are scheduled daily by the shop foreman, work exclusively for the Business and are paid hourly; no written contractor agreements exist for them.

**Why:** On the data room's own facts the flat rep is false: individuals who work exclusively for one business, on its schedule, with its tools and vehicles, paid hourly, for years, are employees under the common-law control test regardless of label (IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41; Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1; worker_classification_tx_irs.md). "1099 forever, everyone does it" (Ray's email) is not a defense. The seller's protection is a disclosure-schedule exception (one of the three recognized routes in sandbagging.md), not a clean rep. Also confirm classification for the 14 W-2 employees — the exception should cover only the 1099 program.

---

## §7.4(a) Basket — **KEEP**

**Buyer's draft:** $75,000 basket, deductible structure ("and then only for Losses in excess of the Basket").

**Why keep:** A deductible basket is a recognized market structure (vs. tipping, where crossing the threshold means paying from dollar one); baskets_caps.md. The deductible form is the seller-favorable one and $75,000 ≈ 2.4% of the implied $3.1M price is an unremarkable level. Known claims (Hardaway $9,800 + warranty log est. $23,000 = $32,800, data room §§5.1–5.2) sit below the basket, so under the deductible they stay with the buyer. Optional nicety: expressly exclude pre-closing warranty items and the Hardaway matter from "Losses" so buyer cannot aggregate them toward the basket.

---

## §7.4(b) Cap — **CHANGE**

**Buyer's draft:** 10% of Purchase Price general cap; Fundamental Representations **and Section 4.12** capped at the full Purchase Price.

**Replacement language (proposed):**

> (b) Seller's aggregate liability under Section 7.1 shall not exceed 10% of the Purchase Price (the "Cap"), except for Fundamental Representations and taxes, which shall be subject to a cap equal to the Purchase Price. Section 4.12 is subject to the general Cap and, in addition, to the Special Contractor Indemnity in new Section 7.5 [below]. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Special Contractor Indemnity cap is $125,000, is excluded from the Basket, survives 30 months after Closing, and is the Buyer's sole remedy for losses arising from worker classification.

# Reply to buyer's counsel (J. Whitaker)

Re: Brightline Cabinetry LLC — asset sale to Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC; response to cover email (Schedule 3.3; WARN; §7.4(c)).

---

## 1. Schedule 3.3 — "we understand there are no consent issues"

That understanding is incorrect. The data room shows two contract consents and one governmental approval:

**(a) Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement (data room §1.1; largest customer, 38% of 2025 revenue — 0.38 × $4.6M ≈ $1,748,000).** MSA §18 bars assignment "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" without prior written consent, "which may be withheld in its sole discretion," and provides that any purported assignment in violation is **void**. A clause in that form is enforced according to its terms; in an asset sale, transferring the contract without consent is a breach and the transfer fails. *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §317; anti_assignment_change_of_control.md. Buyer presumably intends to acquire this contract — §3.1 covers the Assigned Contracts — so Hensley's written consent belongs on Schedule 3.3 and, in our view, in the closing conditions. Because consent is in Hensley's sole discretion, we flag now that Hensley may seek commercial concessions; who bears that cost is a deal term, not something a blank schedule resolves.

**(b) Shop lease, 7700 Burleson Rd (data room §3.1, lease §22).** Landlord consent required, not to be unreasonably withheld. Belongs on Schedule 3.3.

**(c) Cascade Builders (data room §1.2; 11% of revenue).** No consent required — assignment is permitted to a successor to substantially all assets upon notice. We will give written notice; no closing condition needed.

**(d) 22 residential contracts (data room §1.3; each <$40k).** Silent on assignment. Absent anti-assignment language, assignment of contract rights is generally permitted, and delegation of duties requires consent only where performance is personal. Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§317, 322; anti_assignment_change_of_control.md. No consents expected; we ask your client to accept a confirmation that no engagement is personal-services dependent (we are verifying on our side).

**(e) City of Austin spray-booth permit (data room §4.1).** Not an assignment issue — the permit is non-transferable and Buyer must reapply (30–60 days). This should be handled as a governmental approval in Schedule 3.3/closing mechanics, with the application filed pre-closing; it is on the critical path against your two-week signing target.

Proposed response: we will circulate a populated Schedule 3.3 (items (a), (b), (e), with (c) as a notice item). A "commercially reasonable efforts" covenant pointed at a schedule reading "None" protects no one and does not change what your client actually acquires.

## 2. WARN — "can you confirm headcount is under threshold?"

Confirmed on the data room census (data room §§2.1–2.2): **14 W-2 employees** (7 shop + 4 installers + 3 office). WARN applies to employers of **100 or more employees** (excluding part-time) and to plant closings or mass layoffs affecting 50+ employees at a single site; Texas has no mini-WARN statute. 29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1); 20 C.F.R. §639.3; warn_act.md. Brightline is not a covered employer, so no WARN notice is required — including if your client does not hire every employee.

One caveat stated for the record: this conclusion does not depend on the worker-classification debate. Even counting the nine 1099 installers as employees (14 + 9 = 23), the business remains far below the 100-employee threshold. So your client's plan to issue no WARN notices is fine at this size — but it is fine because of headcount, not because classification is settled (see §3 and our redlines).

## 3. Our position on §7.4(c) (sandbagging)

We do not accept §7.4(c) as drafted, and we do not agree it is a neutral "simplification to market-standard knowledge language."

As drafted it is a **pro-sandbagging** clause: Buyer keeps full indemnity rights "regardless of knowledge acquired (or capable of being acquired) at any time, whether before or after execution." That includes everything in our data room. Under Delaware and Texas practice, a seller who discloses a known issue in diligence and then gives a clean representation subject to a pro-sandbagging clause has effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue; the recognized seller protections are an anti-sandbagging clause, a disclosure-schedule exception, or a special indemnity with a negotiated cap. sandbagging.md (*Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta); ABA Private Target Deal Points Study). Market practice is split, not uniformly pro-sandbagging.

The problem is concrete, not theoretical. Your draft pairs §7.4(c) with (i) a clean §4.12 classification rep, (ii) a §7.4(b) carve-out putting §4.12 at a **full-purchase-price cap** (≈$3.1M on the implied price), and (iii) §7.4(d) survival to the statute of limitations. Your client's data room (data room §2.2: nine installers, exclusive, company tools/trucks, foreman-scheduled, hourly, $612,000 of 1099 payments in 2025) already shows these workers are employees under the common-law control test (IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41; worker_classification_tx_irs.md). The combined effect is that Ray indemnifies Lone Star — up to the entire price, personally, for 6+ years — for a problem Lone Star already knows about, with no dollar-matched security. A specific operational rep carved out to a full-price cap is also off-market; the market answer is a sized special indemnity. baskets_caps.md.

**Our proposal:**
1. §4.12 becomes "except as set forth on Schedule 4.12," with the installer program disclosed on that schedule;
2. §7.4(c) becomes anti-sandbagging (no recovery for inaccuracy of a representation Buyer actually knew pre-closing, including from the data room and schedules) — fallback: pro-sandbagging except for matters disclosed in the data room or schedules;
3. §4.12 comes back under the general 10% cap; worker classification moves to a **special indemnity sized to the exposure** (we are prepared to discuss a cap in the $75k–$150k range, 30-month survival, secured within the existing escrow), instead of the full-price carve-out.

If Lone Star wants certainty on the classification issue, that is a price/special-indemnity conversation we can have openly — it should not be papered as a clean rep plus a knowledge-blind indemnity.

We also note §2.4 (EBITDA "as determined by Buyer") and §8.2 (7 years/500 miles) remain open; see our redline for proposed language on each (earnout: *Lazard Technology Partners v. Qinetiq*, 114 A.3d 193 (Del. 2015); non-compete: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50; *Marsh USA v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)).

# Note to Ray — what could cost you money after closing

Plain English. Ray is selling Brightline Cabinetry to Lone Star Millwork; the buyer's paper is their standard form, and three things in it are wired to bill you after closing, on paper you already have in the data room.

(Assumption we could not confirm from the file: the price is about **$3.1M**, because the escrow says $310,000 = "10%". Tell us if the real number is different — everything below scales with it.)

## 1. The 1099 installers — this is the big one

Your nine installers are 1099s on paper only. They work only for you, show up on the foreman's daily schedule, drive your trucks and use your tools, and get paid hourly. Under the IRS test that makes them employees no matter what the forms say — "everyone in the industry does it" is not a defense; the label is the last thing a court looks at, not the first.

Rough cost if the government reclassifies: on the $612,000 you paid them in 2025, employer payroll tax alone is about $18,500/year even at the reduced "non-willful" rates, roughly $57,000 over three years — before interest, penalties, Texas unemployment tax, overtime (they're hourly; we don't have their hours), benefits claims, and workers' comp.

Now look at the buyer's draft: it makes you **represent** everyone is properly classified (it isn't), caps your liability on that one rep at the **whole purchase price (~$3.1M)** instead of the normal 10% ($310k), keeps it alive for **years past the 18-month escrow**, and includes a clause (§7.4(c)) saying the buyer can collect **even though they already read about the installers in your data room**. Stacked together: a disclosed, ~$50k–$150k problem becomes a personal claim worth up to $3.1M.

**Fix before signing:** disclose the installers on a schedule attached to that rep, and replace the full-price clause with a special indemnity sized to the real exposure (we suggest $75k–$150k cap, tied to the escrow). If the buyer wants to reclassify them going forward, fine — that's their business; your cost must be capped.

## 2. Hensley Homes can blow up the sale — or re-price it

Your biggest customer (38% of revenue, ~$1.75M/yr) has a contract that says no assignment in an asset sale without **their written consent, which they can refuse for any reason**, and that any assignment made anyway is **void**. The buyer's draft lists **zero** required consents — their schedule literally says "None." If you close without Hensley's signature, the buyer doesn't get the contract they paid for, and they will come back to you under the indemnity for the difference. And because Hensley can say no freely, expect them to ask for better terms in exchange for the consent.

**Fix:** get Hensley's written consent (and the landlord's consent to assign the shop lease — easier, the lease says consent can't be unreasonably withheld) **before closing**, as a condition, and decide in advance what concession, if any, you'll pay Hensley to keep the deal moving. Also start the spray-booth permit re-application now (30–60 days; the permit does not transfer) or the buyer may not be able to legally run the booth at closing — that's a schedule problem against a two-week signing.

## 3. The earn-out is mostly decoration — don't pay for it with real terms

The earn-out pays you 40% of next year's EBITDA **above $700,000**, max $400,000. Do the math: to collect the full $400k, EBITDA must hit **$1,700,000** — more than double your best year ($740k, and that number only works because you add back your salary and legal fees; on the raw books it's $518k, *below* the hurdle). At your current level the payout is 40% × ($740k − $700k) = **$16,000**. And the draft says EBITDA is "determined by Buyer" under the Buyer's own accounting rules — meaning they can bury the business in overhead and integration charges and pay zero legitimately.

**Fix:** either fix the definition (neutral accounting rules, buyer's overhead and deal costs excluded, audit rights, neutral accountant decides disputes, full payment if they resell) — or, more honestly, treat the earn-out as worth close to nothing and push for more cash at closing. Don't give up indemnity protections in exchange for an earn-out that was never going to pay.

## Two smaller things (won't cost you much, but don't sign blind)

- **Non-compete:** 7 years / 500 miles is almost certainly too broad for a shop like yours in Texas — a court would shrink it. Since you're retiring it barely restrains you, so the real trap is tax: if any of the price (the library notes a $400k allocation, "see tax engagement" — we don't have that document) is pinned to that covenant, an overbroad covenant invites IRS scrutiny of the split. Push it to 3–5 years, Austin-area counties, and confirm with your tax person how the price is being allocated before you sign.
- **Good news, for once:** WARN (the 60-day layoff notice law) doesn't apply — you have 14 employees, the law starts at 100, Texas has no state version. Even counting the installers, 23 < 100. The buyer asked us to confirm; we have.

**One-line answer to "what bites me later":** the installer classification rep with the full-price cap and knowledge-blind indemnity; the Hensley consent the buyer pretends isn't needed; and an earn-out that pays nothing unless you fix its definition. Fix all three in the paper now — after signing, they're your bills, not the buyer's.
